opus-5.5.text:
I think it's useful to separate what we've actually seen from what we hope to see.

What we've observed is that when you train a single model on data from several different robot embodiments, say a bimanual platform, a single-arm robot, and a humanoid, the skills learned on one body start showing up on another. A task that only ever appeared in data collected on robot A can be performed, at least partially, on robot B, even though robot B never saw a demonstration of it. That's what we mean by motion transfer. It's not copying joint trajectories, because the kinematics are completely different. The model seems to learn something more abstract: what it means to grasp, to fold, to push something into place. Then it re-expresses that intent through whatever body it's controlling.

So the scope right now is roughly this. Transfer works best between embodiments that are reasonably similar in how they interact with the world. Two-fingered or simple grippers, arms with comparable workspaces, similar camera viewpoints. Semantic and task-level knowledge transfers quite well. Fine-grained dexterity and contact-rich control transfer much less, because those depend heavily on the specific hardware: the friction of the fingertips, the compliance of the joints, the torque limits. You can't fully abstract those away.

I'd also be careful not to overclaim. This isn't zero-shot onto any arbitrary robot. If you bring in a radically new body, like a legged mobile manipulator with a very different morphology, you still need some data from that body. What changes is how much. Instead of thousands of hours you might need far less, because the model already brings a prior about how manipulation should go.

How I personally see it: it's similar to what happened in language models. Training across many languages helped low-resource languages, because there's a shared structure underneath. In robotics, the shared structure is physics and task semantics, and the different bodies are like different languages. The more embodiments we include, the more the model is forced to learn what's common rather than what's specific. I think that's one of the most promising paths toward a true robot foundation model, because no single robot will ever have enough data on its own. Data from every robot has to be able to help every other robot.

r001.rationale: The response says this is not zero-shot onto any arbitrary robot and that a radically new body still needs some data from that body.

r002.rationale: It explains that a task demonstrated only on robot A can be performed at least partially by robot B, which never saw a demonstration of it.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because "generalization" gets used very loosely in robotics, and motion transfer is a good place to be precise about it.

The way I see it, there are really three different axes you can generalize along, and they're not equally hard.

The first is across robots within the same morphology family. Take legged locomotion. If you've trained a policy on one quadruped and want it to work on a different quadruped with a different leg length, a different mass distribution, different actuators, that's actually quite tractable now. The underlying dynamics are similar enough that if you randomize over kinematic and dynamic parameters during training, or condition the policy on a morphology descriptor, you get a single controller that handles a whole range of bodies. We've seen this work fairly convincingly, and I'd say that part is close to solved in simulation, and reasonably solved in the real world for a few families.

The second axis is across morphologies, like going from a quadruped to a humanoid, or from a legged robot to a wheeled-legged hybrid. Here the generalization is much shallower than people sometimes claim. What transfers is not really the motor commands, it's the higher-level structure of the behavior: things like contact scheduling, center-of-mass regulation, how you shift weight before you swing a limb. So the honest framing is that we transfer motion intent or motion priors, and then a substantial amount of adaptation still has to happen for the new body. Retargeting from human motion capture to a humanoid is a nice example. The data gives you the "what," and you still need learning or optimization to figure out the "how" for that specific set of joints and actuators.

The third axis, and the one I find most interesting, is generalization across tasks and environments once you have transferred a motion. A policy that imitates walking on one robot and then has to walk on gravel, or carry a payload, or recover from a push. That's where you find out whether the transfer produced something robust or something brittle that happens to match a reference trajectory.

So if someone asks "does motion transfer generalize," my answer is: yes, quite well within a morphology class, partially across morphologies in the sense of transferring structure rather than control, and the real test is whether the result stays robust under new tasks. I'm optimistic because the trend is clearly toward larger and more diverse training distributions, and in my experience diversity in the embodiment distribution is what ultimately buys you generalization. But I try to be careful not to oversell it. A video of one robot doing one motion that was retargeted from another robot is impressive, but it is a demonstration, not generalization. Generalization is what happens on the robot you didn't train on, doing the thing you didn't anticipate.

r001.rationale: The response says that across morphologies, substantial adaptation is still needed for the new body, so transferring motion does not by itself establish that the robot can perform it without further training or adaptation.

r002.rationale: The response discusses transferring motion structure and testing robustness on new tasks, but does not state that a robot represented in training can perform a task unseen for it because that task was demonstrated on another robot.

astra-6.text:
I think motion transfer across robots demonstrates one important dimension of generalization: whether a motion or a skill learned on one body can be adapted to another body. Different robots may have different limb lengths, joint limits, degrees of freedom, and dynamics, so transferring a motion successfully means handling some of those differences while preserving the intent of the behavior.

But we should be precise about how broad that generalization is. Transferring between two robots with similar structures is different from transferring between very different morphologies. And if each new robot requires substantial tuning or additional training, that is useful adaptation, but it is different from a system that can control an unseen robot immediately.

So I would view motion transfer as progress toward general-purpose robot control, but not as evidence of generalization across everything. Generalizing across bodies, across tasks, and across environments are distinct challenges. Success on one does not automatically imply success on the others.

r001.rationale: The response says that requiring tuning or additional training is different from controlling an unseen robot immediately, so motion transfer alone does not establish training-free performance on a new robot.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes generalization across bodies and tasks, but does not state that a robot seen during training can perform a task unseen for it after that task was demonstrated on another robot.

sol-6.1.text:
I think motion transfer gives us an important form of generalization, but we should be precise about what generalizes. If a motion learned on one robot can be adapted to another robot with different body proportions or dynamics, then we’re generalizing across embodiments. The goal is to preserve the intent of the motion, rather than copy every joint angle.

But that doesn’t automatically mean the robot can handle new tasks or new environments. Transferring a walking motion to another robot is one capability; knowing how to walk over an unfamiliar obstacle is another. So I would view motion transfer as a building block toward more general robot intelligence, with its scope depending on how different the robots are and how much adaptation the transfer requires.

r001.rationale: The response says motion transfer does not automatically enable new tasks or environments, but it does not state that a new robot cannot perform the transferred tasks without training.

r002.rationale: It describes adapting a learned motion across robots, but not a robot represented in training data generalizing to a task unseen for it after that task is demonstrated on another robot.
